spec.title: Offered vs handled rate (req/s)
spec.description: Offered = iterations k6 started + dropped (what k6 tried to send). Handled = what the server answered, split into 202 and everything else. Look for: the 202 line leaving the offered line (that is the capacity). Surprising: a flat 202 line while offered keeps rising means a hard ceiling; offered itself below the step target means k6 was the problem (see row 4). k6 series are not marked stale after a run, so values can linger for minutes.

spec.title: Error rate: k6 not-202 share and server 5xx share
spec.description: k6 side counts anything that is not 202 as failed (script.js sets expectedStatuses(202)). Server side is the share of 5xx. My collapse rule is more than 1% (0.01). Expect 503 (pool timeout 2 s or DB error). Surprising: k6 share much higher than server share = requests that never got an answer (timeouts, connection errors).

spec.title: Latency seen by k6: p50 / p99 / p99.9
spec.description: Native-histogram form of k6_http_req_duration_seconds (the inventory shows no _bucket series). Flat then bending sharply = the knee. Note k6 latency includes the generator side. Surprising: p99 rising long before p50 = queueing starting for some requests only. Top bucket may clamp very large values.

spec.title: k6 p99 by step (offered_rate tag)
spec.description: One line per step rate. Read the legend max column: this is the p99-vs-rate curve for the baseline report. The label comes from options.tags in script.js; repeats of the same rate share one label, so use runs.tsv to tell repeats apart.

spec.title: Server-side latency p50 / p99 (route histogram)
spec.description: Measured inside Express by the metrics middleware (starts before the body parser, ends when the response closes). Compare with the k6 panel: the gap is network + queueing before the middleware + generator time. Surprising: server p99 flat but k6 p99 rising = the wait happens before Node sees the request (event loop busy, accept queue).

spec.title: Responses by status (server)
spec.description: 202 should dominate until the knee; then 503 appears (pool wait timeout 2 s, statement timeout 5 s, DB errors). Surprising: 500 (unhandled error) or 4xx (validation, 413) - that would be a bug in my test, not the collapse.

spec.title: Pool state (pg.Pool)
spec.description: total = connections opened (max is PG_POOL_MAX, default 10), idle = free, waiting = requests queued inside Node for a connection. If total sits at the max and waiting climbs, the pool is the limit. Surprising: waiting stays 0 while latency rises = the limit is somewhere else (Node CPU or Postgres time per query).

spec.title: Pool wait vs query time (p50 / p99)
spec.description: Request latency is roughly pool wait + query time + Node work. Query time = INSERT on an acquired connection. If wait grows and query stays flat, I am queueing on the pool, not slow in Postgres (Stage 1 pitfall: do not mistake client queueing for database slowness). If query time itself grows, Postgres is saturated (CPU, commit/fsync or locks).

spec.title: In-flight requests vs Little's Law
spec.description: Little's Law: in-flight = rate x mean latency. The measured line (http_requests_in_flight) should sit on the computed line. If measured is much higher, requests are stuck waiting (queue building). Surprising: the two lines disagree even at low load = a metric problem (check the route filter).

spec.title: Pool-bound ceiling: pool max / mean query time (req/s)
spec.description: If every request needs one of 10 connections for its whole query, throughput cannot exceed 10 / mean query time. ASSUMES PG_POOL_MAX=10: edit the 10 in this query if I change POOL_MAX. Compare with the 202 rate: if 202/s hits this line at the knee, the pool is the limit; if the knee is far below, something else bends first.

spec.title: Inserts, duplicates and DB errors (per second)
spec.description: inserted should match 202/s. duplicates should be 0 (every event_id is unique). db_errors are requests answered 503 because of pool or DB trouble. Surprising: any duplicates = my k6 uuid generator is repeating ids; inserted below 202 = rows lost (the audit in step.sh will also say LOST).

spec.title: Node process CPU (cores)
spec.description: user + system CPU of the ingest-api process, in cores (1.0 = one core fully busy). Node runs JS on one thread, so about 1.0 means the event loop thread is saturated (server is pinned to CPUs 0,6 = one physical core, so the ceiling is ~1.0 plus a little GC/libuv). Surprising: well below 1.0 at the knee = Node is NOT the limit.

spec.title: Event loop delay
spec.description: How late the event loop runs its callbacks. Near 0 while healthy; rising p99/max = the JS thread is busy (CPU-bound) or blocked. Note: the Stage 1 metric resets its histogram on each scrape.

spec.title: Postgres container CPU (cores)
spec.description: MISSING until pg-container-exporter.sh runs (see missing-metrics.txt). CPU of the whole Postgres container (all backends), in cores. The container has cpus: 2, so 2.0 is its ceiling. Surprising: near 2.0 = Postgres CPU is the limit; low CPU but high latency = waiting on fsync/locks, not computing.

spec.title: Postgres CPU vs its limit
spec.description: MISSING until the exporter runs. Total container CPU (cores) and the throttled time per second. Throttled > 0 means the cpus: 2 limit paused the container, which adds latency even if the host has free cores.

spec.title: Postgres container memory
spec.description: MISSING until the exporter runs. Container memory (limit mem_limit: 2g). Growth over a run is cache and connection memory; near the limit would cause OOM kills (surprising).

spec.title: Postgres container disk write / read (bytes/s)
spec.description: MISSING until the exporter runs. Bytes the container writes to disk per second (WAL + data files + checkpoint bursts). Spikes every few minutes are checkpoints. Compare with the host disk panels below.

spec.title: Host CPU busy by component (pinned CPU groups)
spec.description: Busy share of the CPUs each component is pinned to: server 0,6; postgres 1,7,2,8; k6 3,9,4,10; monitoring 5,11 (the label values are the logical CPU numbers). The component whose group hits ~100% first is a candidate bottleneck. Assumes the pinning in step.sh was applied. Server uses one core = 2 logical CPUs, so one busy JS thread shows as about 50% here.

spec.title: Host disk utilization (io_time share)
spec.description: Share of each second a disk had I/O in flight (the iostat %util idea). I do not know which device holds the Docker volume, so all devices are shown: the busy one is the Postgres disk. Near 1.0 = disk saturated (commit fsync cost). NVMe can show 1.0 while still having headroom (not verified), so read it together with write await.

spec.title: Host disk write latency (await, seconds)
spec.description: Mean time per completed write = write_time / writes completed. Rising await at the knee means commits wait longer for the disk (fsync). Surprising: flat await while Postgres query time rises = the cost is CPU or locks, not the disk.

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations (must be 0)
spec.description: Requests k6 wanted to send but could not (no free VU). 0 is required for a trusted step. If > 0 look at the k6 CPU panel: generator at its CPU limit = discard the step; generator fine but all VUs waiting = the server is so slow that this is part of the collapse (note it, do not hide it).

spec.title: k6 VUs vs max VUs
spec.description: Active VUs. Little's Law again: VUs needed = rate x latency. A line touching vus_max means the cap (MAX_VUS, default 3000) is limiting the generator.

spec.title: Generator CPU busy (k6 CPUs, keep < 70%)
spec.description: Busy share of the CPUs k6 is pinned to (3,9,4,10). Keep under about 70%. Over that the generator may be the bottleneck and the step is not trustworthy.

spec.title: Server open file descriptors and connections
spec.description: process_open_fds and open TCP connections. Surprising: fds close to process_max_fds (Stage 0 lesson). Expect it far below the limit here.

spec.title: Listen queue overflows and drops (per second)
spec.description: Kernel counters for connections refused because the accept queue was full. Should be 0. If > 0 the collapse involves the accept backlog (Stage 0 E0.8), not only the pool.

spec.title: Node heap and RSS
spec.description: Memory of the ingest-api process. Growth during a collapsed step is queued requests/promises piling up in Node (watch for it in B10). Surprising: RSS climbing without end during a steady step.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: where does it bend, and what breaks first?
2. The mechanism: pool, database or Node?
4. Validity checks: can I trust this run?
